Spanish Retail Workers Stage Nationwide Walkout, Disrupting Stores and Sales

Thousands of retail workers across Spain staged a coordinated walkout on Thursday, halting operations at major shopping centers, supermarkets, and flagship stores as part of an ongoing dispute over pay and working conditions. The industrial action, led by the National Retail Employees Confederation (CNCE), is now in its second day and has caused widespread disruption across the country’s retail sector.

According to the CNCE, over 60% of retail staff at participating companies have joined the strike, affecting locations in Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, and Seville. In many city centers, customers encountered shuttered storefronts and lengthy queues at the few shops that remained open with reduced staff. Several major retailers, including Supermercados Rivera and ModaPronto, reported temporary closures of their largest outlets due to the lack of personnel.

“We have been forced to close 80% of our stores nationwide today,” said Javier Ortega, spokesperson for Supermercados Rivera, one of Spain’s largest grocery chains. “Our remaining locations are operating with skeleton crews, and we are already seeing significant declines in daily revenue.” 

Retail analysts estimate that the sector could lose up to €65 million in sales per day if the strike continues at its current scale. “This is the most significant disruption to Spain’s retail sector in at least a decade,” said Marta Benítez, retail analyst at Iberia Market Insights. “With the walkout coinciding with the start of the summer shopping season, the financial impact could be substantial.”

The CNCE is demanding a 12% wage increase over two years, improved job security guarantees for part-time and temporary staff, and stricter enforcement of health and safety regulations in stores and warehouses. Negotiations between union representatives and retail employers’ associations broke down earlier this week, prompting the call for industrial action.

“We regret the inconvenience to customers, but our members have been left with no choice,” said CNCE general secretary Luis Fernández in a statement. “Retail workers have kept these businesses running through challenging times and deserve fair compensation and safe conditions.”

Retail employers’ groups argue that the sector is still recovering from the pandemic’s effects and warn that the demands could put smaller chains at risk. “We are ready to return to negotiations, but the current demands are unsustainable for many businesses,” said Ana Ruiz, president of the Spanish Retailers’ Federation.

As the strike enters its third day, both sides have indicated a willingness to resume talks, though no formal meetings have yet been scheduled. The CNCE has pledged to continue the walkout until an agreement is reached.
